top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures and electron-domain counting to predict electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Explain how lone pairs alter molecular shape and bond angles by increasing electron-pair repulsion.
Match VSEPR predictions to observed shapes of common molecules and recognize the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.

scenes.brief_purpose: Orient students to the core idea that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and adopt arrangements that minimize repulsion.
key_visuals: A central atom surrounded by a few electron-pair regions expanding into 3D space
Simple labels for bonding pairs and lone pairs
A clean comparison between crowded and evenly spaced arrangements
student_actions: Read the prompt and identify the central concept of repulsion among electron pairs.
Select or highlight where electron domains would be placed to make them as far apart as possible.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis structure to electron domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how to count electron domains on a central atom from a Lewis structure and connect that count to the appropriate electron-domain geometry.
key_visuals: Several simple Lewis structures with the central atom emphasized
Electron domains appearing as distinct regions around the central atom
Five named geometry categories represented in a progression from 2 to 6 domains
student_actions: Count bonding and lone-pair domains around the central atom.
Choose the electron-domain geometry that matches the domain count.

scenes.brief_purpose: Walk through the five fundamental geometries and their ideal arrangements so students can build a mental map of shapes in 3D.
key_visuals: Linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements shown one by one
Angle guides and symmetry cues for each geometry
Side-by-side views that reveal the spatial differences among the five geometries
student_actions: Rotate each model and compare the relative positions of domains.
Identify the ideal bond angles for each geometry before adding lone pairs.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that lone pairs take up more space than bonding pairs and therefore compress bond angles and produce common molecular shapes.
key_visuals: Models transforming from electron-domain geometry to molecular geometry
Examples showing bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, and square pyramidal forms
Bond-angle readouts that shift away from ideal values when lone pairs are present
student_actions: Add lone pairs to the central atom and observe how the molecular shape changes.
Compare the resulting shape to the ideal electron-domain arrangement and note which positions lone pairs prefer.

scenes.brief_purpose: Give students hands-on practice arranging electron domains so the model settles into the lowest-repulsion configuration.
key_visuals: Movable electron-domain markers around a central atom
Visual feedback showing domains spacing apart as the model stabilizes
Highlighted lone-pair positions when a correct arrangement is reached
student_actions: Drag electron domains into different positions and test configurations.
Use the repulsion principle to determine the arrangement that minimizes crowding.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect VSEPR predictions to real examples so students see the theory applied to familiar molecules and measured geometries.
key_visuals: Water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 shown as labeled 3D models
Predicted vs. observed geometry displayed together
A comparison of water's smaller bond angle with methane's ideal tetrahedral angle
student_actions: Match each molecule to its predicted molecular geometry.
Compare predicted and observed structures and explain any bond-angle deviations using lone-pair repulsion.
